yv <- paste0("sbp_m", c(0, 1, 3, 6, 9, 12))

::: {.callout-warning title="Simulated data"}
All examples use simulated data from fictional studies. Results illustrate methods; they are not empirical findings.
:::

This knowledge check has 13 questions. Each is mapped to a Module 3 learning outcome. Answer all questions before looking at the final section, which is for instructors.

# Questions

## Question 1 (LO 3.1)

The following model was fitted to the WALK long data.

```{r}
#| label: q1
m <- lm(sbp ~ month * arm, data = walk)
round(coef(summary(m)), 3)
```

What does the coefficient of `armEP` represent?

a. The effect of the enhanced programme on SBP at month 12.
b. The difference in mean SBP between EP and UC at month 0.
c. The average difference in SBP between EP and UC over the year.
d. The difference in mean slope between EP and UC.

## Question 2 (LO 3.1)

Using the output in Question 1, what is the model's estimate of the difference in mean SBP between EP and UC at month 12? Show your calculation.

## Question 3 (LO 3.1)

True or false, with a one-sentence justification: "A residual-versus-fitted plot with no pattern shows that the independence assumption of the model in Question 1 is reasonable."

## Question 4 (LO 3.2)

A paired t-test in the EP arm gives the following output.

```{r}
#| label: q4
ep <- wide |> filter(arm == "EP", !is.na(sbp_m0), !is.na(sbp_m12))
t.test(ep$sbp_m12, ep$sbp_m0, paired = TRUE)
```

Which statement is correct?

a. The enhanced programme reduces SBP by about 10 mmHg compared with usual care.
b. Mean SBP among EP participants with both measurements fell by about 10 mmHg from baseline to month 12.
c. The result shows that the change in EP is larger than the change in UC.
d. The test uses all 120 participants randomised to EP.

## Question 5 (LO 3.2)

Name two assumptions of a paired t-test and one reason why WALK participants with both baseline and month-12 measurements may not represent all randomised participants.

## Question 6 (LO 3.2, 3.3)

The output below is from a repeated-measures ANOVA on completers.

```{r}
#| label: q6
cc <- wide[complete.cases(wide[, yv]), ]
Y <- as.matrix(cc[, yv])
mlm <- lm(Y ~ arm, data = cc)
idata <- data.frame(visit = factor(yv, levels = yv))
q6 <- anova(mlm, X = ~1, idata = idata, test = "Spherical")
q6
```

Which row tests whether the change in SBP over time differs between arms, and what is its Greenhouse–Geisser corrected p-value?

## Question 7 (LO 3.3)

Which statement best describes sphericity?

a. All measurements have the same variance.
b. The variance of the difference between any two occasions is the same for every pair of occasions.
c. The residuals are normally distributed at every occasion.
d. The correlation between occasions decreases with the time between them.

## Question 8 (LO 3.3)

The Greenhouse–Geisser epsilon in Question 6 is `r f2(as.numeric(sub(".*: *", "", grep("Greenhouse", attr(q6, "heading"), value = TRUE))))`. What would an epsilon of exactly 1 mean, and what does the correction do to the F-test?

## Question 9 (LO 3.3)

List three limitations of repeated-measures ANOVA for the WALK data that the Greenhouse–Geisser correction does **not** fix.

## Question 10 (LO 3.4)

Three analyses of month-12 SBP gave these results for EP versus UC.

```{r}
#| label: q10
#| echo: false
d12 <- wide |> filter(!is.na(sbp_m0), !is.na(sbp_m12)) |> mutate(chg = sbp_m12 - sbp_m0)
q10 <- bind_rows(
  fixef_table(lm(sbp_m12 ~ arm, data = d12)) |> mutate(analysis = "B"),
  fixef_table(lm(chg ~ arm, data = d12)) |> mutate(analysis = "C"),
  fixef_table(lm(sbp_m12 ~ arm + sbp_m0, data = d12)) |> mutate(analysis = "A")) |>
  filter(term == "armEP") |> select(analysis, estimate, se) |> arrange(analysis)
q10
```

Analyses A, B and C are follow-up only, change score and ANCOVA, in some order. The correlation between baseline and month-12 SBP is `r f2(cor(d12$sbp_m0, d12$sbp_m12))`. Which is which? Explain using the standard errors.

## Question 11 (LO 3.4)

True or false, with justification: "In a randomised trial, change-score analysis and ANCOVA estimate different treatment effects, so the choice between them depends on which effect you want."

## Question 12 (LO 3.4)

In an observational study, men and women are compared on blood pressure measured at two times. A change-score analysis shows no difference between sexes, while ANCOVA adjusting for the first measurement shows a clear difference. Name this phenomenon and explain briefly why it occurs.

## Question 13 (LO 3.5)

An analysis plan proposes comparing each of two programmes with usual care by t-test at each of six visits. Give three reasons why this is inadequate, and state the probability of at least one false-positive result if the 12 tests were independent and no effect existed.

# Answers and explanations (for instructors)

```{r}
#| label: answers
#| include: false
b <- coef(m)
tt <- t.test(ep$sbp_m12, ep$sbp_m0, paired = TRUE)
eps <- as.numeric(sub(".*: *", "", grep("Greenhouse", attr(q6, "heading"), value = TRUE)))
ord <- q10[order(q10$se), ]
```

**Question 1.** b. With the interaction in the model, `armEP` is the EP–UC difference where `month` = 0 (`r f2(b["armEP"])` mmHg). Option d describes `month:armEP`. (LO 3.1)

**Question 2.** $\hat\beta_{\text{armEP}} + 12\,\hat\beta_{\text{month:armEP}}$ = `r f2(b["armEP"])` + 12 × (`r f2(b["month:armEP"])`) = `r f2(b["armEP"] + 12 * b["month:armEP"])` mmHg. Accept small rounding differences. (LO 3.1)

**Question 3.** False. The residual-versus-fitted plot shows each residual on its own and cannot reveal correlation between residuals from the same participant; that needs, for example, the correlation of residuals across visits, which in WALK is high. (LO 3.1)

**Question 4.** b. The paired test estimates within-arm change among the `r nrow(ep)` EP participants with both measurements (mean change `r f1(tt$estimate)` mmHg). It does not compare arms (a, c) and does not use all randomised participants (d). (LO 3.2)

**Question 5.** Assumptions: independent pairs (participants), approximately normal differences (or a large sample). Representativeness: dropout in WALK depends on the last observed SBP and on arm, so participants with month-12 data are a selected group (MAR dropout). (LO 3.2)

**Question 6.** The row labelled `arm` (contrasts orthogonal to the constant, so arm-by-visit). Greenhouse–Geisser corrected `r fmt_p(q6["arm", "G-G Pr"])`. A common error is to choose the `(Intercept)` row, which tests visit. (LO 3.2, 3.3)

**Question 7.** b. Option a (equal variances) is neither necessary nor sufficient; d describes the pattern that usually *violates* sphericity. (LO 3.3)

**Question 8.** $\epsilon = 1$ means sphericity holds exactly. The correction multiplies both numerator and denominator degrees of freedom by $\hat\epsilon$ (here `r f2(eps)`), which gives a larger p-value and protects against the excess false positives caused by non-sphericity. (LO 3.3)

**Question 9.** Any three of: listwise deletion of participants with any missing visit (`r nrow(wide) - nrow(cc)` of `r nrow(wide)` in WALK); scheduled visits treated as fixed, actual times ignored; no time-varying covariates; no participant-specific slopes; omnibus tests rather than an effect estimate with a CI; requires equal covariance matrices across arms. (LO 3.3)

**Question 10.** The analysis with the largest SE is follow-up only and the smallest is ANCOVA: `r ord$analysis[3]` is follow-up only, `r ord$analysis[2]` is change score and `r ord$analysis[1]` is ANCOVA. With $\rho$ near 0.7, variance is proportional to 1 (follow-up), $2(1-\rho) \approx 0.6$ (change) and $1-\rho^2 \approx 0.5$ (ANCOVA). (LO 3.4)

**Question 11.** False. In a randomised trial both estimate the same treatment effect, because baseline means are equal in expectation; they differ in precision, and ANCOVA is at least as precise [@senn2006; @vickers2001]. (LO 3.4)

**Question 12.** Lord's paradox. The groups differ at baseline and are not randomised. ANCOVA compares people with the same observed first measurement; because of measurement error and regression to the mean, such people from the higher-mean group tend to move up and those from the lower-mean group tend to move down, so ANCOVA finds a difference that the change score does not. The two analyses answer different questions. (LO 3.4)

**Question 13.** Multiplicity (12 tests); inefficiency (each test ignores baseline and other visits); different subsets of participants at each visit because of dropout, so estimates are inconsistent and possibly biased. Probability of at least one false positive with 12 independent tests: $1 - 0.95^{12}$ = `r f2(1 - 0.95^12)`. (LO 3.5)
